Gaura, a species of ox (Bos gaurus), is frequently mentioned
with the Gavaya from the Rigveda^1 onwards.^2 As the Vāja-
saneyi Saṃhitā^3 expressly mentions wild (āraṇya) Gauras, they
[]
must usually have been tame. The female, Gaurī, is also often
referred to.^4 The compound term Gaura-mṛga (‘the Gaura
wild beast’) is sometimes met with.^5
1) i. 16, 5; iv. 21, 8; 58, 2; v. 78, 2;
vii. 69, 6; 98, 1, etc.
2) Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 10;
Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 28; Aitareya
Brāhmaṇa, iii. 34, etc.
3) xiii. 48.
4) Rv. i. 84, 10; iv. 12, 6; ix. 12,
3; and in the obscure verse i. 164,
11.
5) Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 32;
Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, ii. 8.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 83, 224.

Gauri-vīti Śāktya (‘descendant of Śakti’) or Gaurīviti, as
the name is also spelt,^1 is the Ṛṣi, or Seer, of a hymn of the
Rigveda,^2 and is frequently mentioned in the Brāhmaṇas.^3
According to the Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa,^4 he was Prastotṛ at the
Sattra, or sacrificial session, celebrated by the Vibhindukīyas
and mentioned in that Brāhmaṇa.
1) Satapatha Brāhmaṇa, xii. 8, 3, 7;
Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa, xi. 5; xii. 13;
xxv. 7.
2) v. 29, 11.
3) Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, iii. 19; viii. 2
and see n. 1.
4) ii. 233 (Journal of the American
Oriental Society, 18, 38).
Cf. Ludwig, Translation of the Rig-
veda, 3, 126; Oldenberg, Zeitschrift der
Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,
42, 215.
